short.lead: Both versions are built from one set of code. The Windows installer was built and tested on GitHub's own Windows machine: all 40 tests passed there, including the PowerShell limit reporter. Here, the app was driven end to end with three made-up accounts. What's left is your test on your own PC, because some of it only works on a real Windows desktop.
short.hint: Tap an item to see what was checked and what it needs from you.
items: 40 tests pass, on Linux and Windows
Session reading, grouping, context, limits, the reporter (run for real in PowerShell), the board helpers, the walkthrough and the app's account finding and terminal commands.
App driven end to end here

Found three accounts, grouped their sessions into one project, turned on limit tracking (kept the other settings and the old status line), showed a real reading of 93% and 48%, and clicked through the walkthrough. No errors.

items: GitHub built Project Router Setup 0.1.0.exe. The zip you download is 81.7 MB (81,713,063 bytes, from the upload record).
Download it from the link in step 1 of the Wrap-up.
Install, check your three folders are found, resume one session, start one, and turn on limit tracking for one account.
Follow the numbered steps in Wrap-up.

changes: Installer from GitHub; finds folders, resumes and starts sessions.

The Resume and New session here buttons open Windows Terminal (or Command Prompt if Terminal is missing) in the project folder, on the right account. New session picks the account with the lowest 5-hour use; you can change it.
An app in your Start menu.
One click back into any project.

changes.caption: The app's first-run walkthrough, step one.

changes: It publishes from the repository's default branch once GitHub Pages is turned on (Wrap-up step 7) and pull request 9 is merged. You can preview it with made-up data by adding ?demo=1 to the address.
A board in Edge or Chrome.
Works on any PC, without installing anything.

changes.alt: The website board with made-up data: four project columns with coloured stripes and session cards with three bars
changes.caption: The website with made-up data.

changes: It copies settings.json to settings.json.router-backup, saves your old status line, and adds the limit reporter (the small script that saves your 5-hour and weekly use). Turning limit tracking off puts your old status line back.
You see which account has room without checking each one.

wrapup.summary: The router prototype, both website and Windows app, is built and waiting for your test.
wrapup.changing: Pull request 9 (Project Router prototype: website and Windows app) adds the app, the website, the limit reporter, the walkthrough, and two GitHub workflows (automatic jobs that test the code, build the installer and publish the website).
wrapup.blocking: Your test on your PC, and turning on GitHub Pages if you want the website live.
wrapup.next: I fix whatever your test finds. After it passes, you merge the pull request, and the website goes live.
todo: Open the installer download while signed in to GitHub. It downloads project-router-installer.zip.
Unzip it and double-click Project Router Setup 0.1.0.exe. When Windows says "Windows protected your PC", click More info, then Run anyway, and finish the installer.
Open Project Router. Step 1 of the walkthrough should list your three Claude folders. If one is missing, tell me its folder name.
Finish the walkthrough and check that sessions from all three accounts sit together under their project names.
Tap Resume on one session. Windows Terminal should open in that project with the session reopened.
Tap Turn on limit tracking on one account, then send any message in a Claude session on that account. Within 5 seconds the 5-hour and weekly bars should show numbers.
For the website: in the repository on GitHub, open Settings, then Pages, and set Source to GitHub Actions. It goes live once pull request 9 is merged.
When your test is done, tap Copy my reply on this page and send it to me. If something failed, send "QA failed: router windows app" and say what went wrong.
